guarantee.e: From Old French guarantie (perhaps via a later Spanish garante), from the verb guarantir (“to protect, assure, vouch for”), ultimately from Old Frankish *warjand, *warand (“a warrant”), or from guaranty.
guarantee.g: Anything that assures a certain outcome.

guarantor.g: A person, company, or organization that provides a guarantee.

guard.e: From Middle English garde, from early Middle French or late Old French guarde (“a guardian, warden, keeper”) (whence modern French garde), from the verb guarder.
guard.g: A person who, or thing that, protects or watches over something.

guard.e: From early Middle French garder or late Old French (circa 14th cent) guarder (“to keep, ward, guard, save, preserve, etc.”), from Early Medieval Latin wardo, from Frankish *wardēn, from Proto-Germanic *wardāną (“to guard, protect”).
guard.g: To protect from danger; to secure against surprise, attack, or injury; to keep in safety; to defend.

guardian.e: From Middle English gardein, garden, (also wardein, > Modern English warden), from Old French guardein, from the verb guarder, of Germanic origin. By surface analysis, guard + -ian.
guardian.g: Someone who guards, watches over, or protects.

guardroom.g: A room used by soldiers when on guard.

guest.e: From Middle English gest, from Old Norse gestr, which replaced or was merged with Old English ġiest, both from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest, host, someone with whom one has reciprocal duties of hospitality”).
guest.g: A recipient of hospitality, especially someone staying by invitation at the house of another.

guestchamber.e: From Middle English geste-chaumbre, gestchaumbyr, equivalent to guest + chamber.
guestchamber.g: A chamber for the purpose of housing a guest; a guestroom.

guidance.g: The act or process of guiding.

guide.e: From Middle English guide, from the Old French guide, from Old Occitan guida, from guidar, from Frankish *wītan (“to show the way, lead”), from Proto-Germanic *wītaną (“to see, know; go, depart”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, know”). Related also to English wit.
guide.g: Someone who guides, especially someone hired to show people around a place or an institution and offer information and explanation, or to le

guide.e: From Middle English guiden, from Old French guider, from Old Occitan guidar, from Frankish *wītan (“to show the way, lead”), from Proto-Germanic *wītaną (“to see, know; go, depart”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, know”).
guide.g: To serve as a guide for someone or something; to lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path.

guile.e: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”).
guile.g: Astuteness often marked by a certain sense of cunning or artful deception.

guilt.e: From Middle English gilt, gult, from Old English gylt (“guilt, sin, offense, crime, fault”), of obscure origin. Possibly related with Old English ġieldan (“to pay, requite, punish”) (whence yield), from Proto-West Germanic *guldijā (whence Middle High German gülte (“debt, fee, financial duty”), Middle Low German gülde, German Gülte).
From Middle English gilten, gylten, from Old English gyltan (“to commit sin, be guilty”), from gylt (“guilt, sin, offense, crime, fault”).

guiltiness.e: From Middle English giltines; equivalent to guilty + -ness.
guiltiness.g: The state of being guilty; guilt.

guiltless.e: From Middle English giltles, gultles, gyltles, from Old English *gyltlēas, equivalent to guilt + -less.

guilty.e: From Middle English gilty, gulty, from Old English gyltiġ (“offending, guilty”); equivalent to guilt + -y.

gulf.e: From Middle English gulf, goulf, golf, from Old French golf, from Italian golfo, from Late Latin colfos, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, gulf”), of obscure origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve, arch”).
gulf.g: A hollow place in the earth; an abyss; a deep chasm or basin.

gull.e: From Middle English gulle, from a Brythonic language (compare Breton gouelan, Welsh gwylan, and Cornish golan), from Proto-Brythonic *gwuɨlann, from Proto-Celtic *weilannā (“seagull”). Eclipsed Middle English lare (borrowed from Latin larus) and Middle English mewe (from Old English mæw).
gull.g: A seabird of the genus Larus or of the subfamily Larinae.

gull.e: Perhaps from an obsolete term gull (“to swallow, guzzle”), from Middle English golen (“to make swallowing motions, gape”), from Middle English gole (“throat”).

gulp.e: From Middle English gulpen, probably from West Flemish or Middle Dutch gulpen, golpen, of uncertain origin. Perhaps of imitative origin, or related to Dutch galpen (“to roar, squeal”), English galp, gaup (“to gape”).

gum.e: From Middle English gom, gome, gomme, goome, gum, gume, gumme, from Old English gōma (“palate”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōmō, from Proto-Germanic *gaumô, *gōmô (“palate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂- (“to gape, yawn”).

From Middle English gomme, gumme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman gome, from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).
gum.g: A viscous water-soluble carbohydrate exudate of certain plants that hardens when it becomes dry, or such a substance as a component of a pla

gush.e: From Middle English guschen, gusshen, gosshien, perhaps from Middle Dutch guysen (“to flow out with a gurgling sound, gush”) or Old Norse gusa (“to gush”), ultimately imitative.

gutter.e: From Middle English gutter, guttur, goter, from Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere (French gouttière), ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop”).
gutter.g: A prepared channel in a surface, especially at the side of a road adjacent to a curb, intended for the drainage of water.
